analysis.title: September CPI Preview: Renewal of a softer trend
key_insights: Natixis expects September core CPI at 0.19% m/m, in line with consensus, and headline CPI at 0.6% m/m, also in line with consensus.
Those readings would leave core CPI at 2.4% y/y, steady from the prior month, and headline CPI at 3.6% y/y.

August CPI came in above consensus because of education and communication services, which pushed the supercore index to 51bps on the month. Natixis expects those components to give back some of their gains.
If the forecast holds, the 3-month annualized core rate rises to 2.8% as July's negative print drops out, and the 6-month annualized rate falls slightly to 2.55%.
The headline acceleration is mainly an energy and food story tied to renewed geopolitical concerns. Natixis sees no evidence that it is broadening into core prices.

Alternative inflation measures such as trimmed mean and median are trending down. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has alluded to these measures as 'underlying inflation', and the Fed's inflation task force may give them a bigger role.
Inflation breadth was improving until the second half of 2025, when the 'Liberation Day' tariffs took effect. The energy shock after the start of the Iran War added another supply-driven bump.

The SF Fed splits core PCE into cyclical and acyclical components. Acyclical, one-off shocks such as tariffs and energy are mainly keeping inflation elevated, and these respond less to monetary policy.

Natixis expects core goods prices to stay subdued because tariff passthrough is largely behind us. Shelter indicators have stabilized, and core services excluding housing track wage growth that is consistent with target inflation.
Natixis forecasts only one more Fed hike, and says September may have been the lone hike of the cycle. It pencils in another hike in December or January.

Markets have cut the probability of an October hike from about 70% in late September to about 20%. Natixis thinks skipping October is prudent because it allows more data before the December meeting and avoids the political fallout of hiking just before the early-November mid-term elections.

risk_factors: Month-to-month CPI data can be noisy, and it is hard to string together a series of better prints.
Headline inflation could broaden into core if energy and food supply shocks pass through.
Tensions with Canada could revive tariff effects.
A hike just before the early-November mid-term elections carries political fallout.
geopolitical: Renewed geopolitical concerns are pushing up energy and food prices and headline CPI.
The energy shock followed the start of the Iran War.
Tariff passthrough is largely behind us, though tensions with Canada continue.
The 'Liberation Day' tariffs lifted price levels in the second half of 2025.

tension_points.bull_case: Natixis expects subdued core prints to support only one more hike. September may have been the lone hike, and core goods, shelter and non-housing services are all stable.
tension_points.bear_case: Influential Fed policymakers suggest more hikes are likely given the uncertainty. Month-to-month data is noisy, and Natixis itself pencils in another hike in December or January.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A string of upside core CPI prints, as August showed, would push the Fed toward further hikes.

theme_stances.key_argument: Underlying inflation continues to move in the right direction, and August's upside surprise came from components Natixis expects to reverse.
theme_stances.evidence: underlying inflation continues to move in the right direction

theme_stances.key_argument: The Fed will skip October and hike again in December or January, which would complete a short tightening cycle.
